caveats: M1 is NOT a frozen-decoder baseline: the Stage-2 model already fine-tuned its decoder end to end on the predicted z (L_C + 1.0 L_z). M2 differs from M1 in three things changed together (2 extra decoder blocks at width 256, a longer schedule with no stop before 25 000 steps, selection on validation L_C instead of L_C + L_z), not in 'joint versus frozen'; the three are not separated from each other.

The TACO verdict is a close call: the interval excludes 0 and the size (1.96 %) is just under the 2 % threshold; the report says a second training seed could move it to either side. Every model has one training seed; intervals describe the test takes, not training randomness.

The TACO gain is absent at a matched step (M2's state at step 4000 is +0.46 % against M1, similar); the report states this does not cleanly separate selection from capacity. That the gain 'travels with the predicted z, not the decoder' is the report's reading of the swapped-decoder table (old decoder on M2's latents 1.693 against 1.732 on its own); no paired test of that exact comparison exists in the tables.

'Similar' applies to the dense error. Resolved secondary differences exist: participation Hamming is better on both datasets (rel 0.0216 TACO, 0.0485 ARCTIC), frames 1-8 are better on both (0.0400, 0.0393), and on ARCTIC the deviation of the frame-to-frame dense change from the true one is worse (-0.169).

'Longer budget' needs its qualifier: both M2 runs stopped by the patience rule at 25 000 steps (the earliest allowed) and the selected states are step 7000 (TACO) and 8000 (ARCTIC); M1 ran 20 000 (TACO) and 18 000 (ARCTIC, stopped by hand) and was selected at step 4000.

Untested: a wider decoder (the plan recommended 512-768), the 4-block control under the M2 protocol, and a decoder trained on many held-out predictions. The source conclusion is 'no evidence that decoder mismatch caused the failure', not 'decoder mismatch is excluded'.
The unpaired per-model intervals overlap heavily; the test is the paired difference.

caveats: The teacher z* is computed from the TRUE future frames; it is a diagnostic input and a training target, never available at generation time, so 0.51 / 0.69 is a decoder floor, not an achievable generator error.
'0.51 / 0.69' is the new decoder (0.5051 / 0.6936); through the old decoder the same teacher latent gives 0.5100 / 0.7086.

The decoder is sensitive to latent error: random perturbations of the teacher latent of the same size as the model's test error already give 78-84 % (TACO) and 84-90 % (ARCTIC) of the predicted-latent error. These shares are of the predicted-latent error, not of the teacher-to-predicted gap. The report therefore states that the study 'cannot separate the latent error from the decoder's sensitivity to it, because a decoder trained on held-out predictions was not tested'.

The model's own latent errors cost somewhat more than random errors of the same size (TACO both perturbations 'better' than the predicted latent; ARCTIC the Gaussian perturbation through the old decoder is only 'similar', interval [-0.347, +0.058]).
The perturbation is one level only (matched to each model's own test error), one draw.
One training seed per model.

caveats: The bottleneck statement is hedged in the source: Appendix B Q5 'Most likely yes ... The study cannot separate the latent error from the decoder's sensitivity to it, because a decoder trained on held-out predictions was not tested. A second, smaller part is the first frames, where the latent path cannot continue s_0.'

Joint training exposed the decoder to test-sized latent errors only in roughly its first thousand steps (training L_z 0.45 / 0.53 at step 1000 against 0.49 / 0.51 on test; 0.12 / 0.11 at step 2000); the report's wording is that 'trained on predicted z' therefore did not amount to 'adapted to the held-out predicted-z distribution'. Do not say the decoder never saw such errors.
The training-subset values come from 160 fixed random training sequences and have no interval; the teacher z* is a diagnostic input never available at generation time.
On the ARCTIC training subset the predicted z decodes slightly lower than the teacher z* (0.217 against 0.234); on TACO slightly higher (0.193 against 0.179).
One training seed. The stateful-z follow-up is a motivated current hypothesis proposed by the report ('Proposed, not shown'), not a result of this study.
entries.claim_as_extracted: On training sequences the predicted z decodes almost as well as the teacher z* (new decoder: 0.193 against 0.179 on TACO, 0.217 against 0.234 on ARCTIC), whereas on test sequences it decodes at 1.698 against 0.505 and 2.158 against 0.694; this suggests that the remaining error is associated with predicting the whole future z trajectory of unseen sequences, which the report rates as 'most likely' the remaining bottleneck without being able to separate it from the decoder's sensitivity to latent error.
entries.correction_reason: All numbers exact. 'Almost as well as' has the wrong direction for ARCTIC, where the predicted z decodes slightly lower than the teacher z* on the training subset. The training values come from 160 sequences without an interval and that should be in the sentence. Also visible in the same table and not to be hidden: the teacher-z* error itself is about three times higher on test than on the training subset (0.179 vs 0.505 TACO, 0.234 vs 0.694 ARCTIC), so the train-test difference of the decoded error is not only the latent's.

entries.claim: Two small post-hoc probes that fitted the decoder side to the temporal network's validation latents found no gain on either dataset: when the whole decoder was fine-tuned, the out-of-fold validation error rose within the first 100 steps, so zero steps were chosen and the test error is unchanged by construction; five fitted shrinkage factors changed the test error by 0.000 (TACO) and +0.001 (ARCTIC, interval includes 0). The report states that the fine-tuning probe 'cannot bound what a decoder trained on many held-out predictions could do'; such a decoder was not tested.

Probe B: the decoder is untouched, one shrinkage factor of the predicted z per horizon bin (grid 0.5 to 1.0) is chosen on validation. E_C lower is better; test differences are paired with 95 % take-cluster bootstrap intervals.

entries.claim_as_extracted: Two small post-hoc probes that fitted the decoder side to the temporal network's validation latents (fine-tuning the whole decoder; fitting five shrinkage factors) found no test gain on either dataset, and the report states they cannot bound what a decoder trained on many held-out predictions could do.
entries.correction_reason: heldout_probe.csv: s_star 0 on both datasets, so no adapted decoder was ever scored on test ('no test gain' is trivially true and could be read as a tested failure). The quoted 'cannot bound' sentence in report section 12 is about probe A only; for probe B the report says 'A scalar shrinkage of the latent does not help. Other forms of hedging were not tried.' Probes used 141 (TACO) / 106 (ARCTIC) validation sequences.

dataset_differences: Only TACO and ARCTIC exist in this study; there is no OakInk2 result for these blocks.

M2 vs M1 dense error: TACO -0.034 [-0.050, -0.017], a 1.96 % reduction whose interval excludes 0 but which is under the 2 % threshold ('similar', close call); ARCTIC +0.002 [-0.026, +0.032] (-0.08 %, interval includes 0).

M2 vs M0 dense error: TACO 'similar' (+0.15 %, -0.003 [-0.038, +0.038]); ARCTIC 'worse' (-14.19 %, +0.268 [+0.196, +0.344]). M1 vs M0 was already 'similar' on TACO (-1.85 %) and 'worse' on ARCTIC (-14.10 %).
Structural / wrench metrics of M2 vs M0: TACO 4 better / 0 worse of 5 (participation +8.7 %, centroid +7.7 %, normal +2.9 %, wrench +4.0 %; amount similar); ARCTIC 0 better / 1 worse (amount -8.1 %).
Result case of the study's rule (fixed in advance, according to the report): TACO C+D (structure better than direct, dense similar, no gain over M1); ARCTIC D+E (no gain over M1, worse than direct).

Horizon: on TACO M2 is worse than M0 in frames 1-8 (-36.5 %) and 9-16 (-6.7 %), similar in 17-32 and better in 33-48 (+4.0 %) and 49-63 (+4.5 %); on ARCTIC M2 is worse than M0 in every bin (-45.6 % down to -8.1 %).

Selected checkpoint: on TACO the two selection criteria differ (step 7000 on validation L_C, step 4000 on L_C + L_z) and the matched-step comparison with M1 exists; on ARCTIC both criteria chose step 8000, so the sensitivity row is the same state.

Latent error by split (M2): TACO train 0.088, validation 0.630, test 0.702 (validation below test); ARCTIC train 0.064, validation 0.803, test 0.717 (validation above test). Report prose: validation error 7 times (TACO) and 13 times (ARCTIC) the training error.
Predictability of the held-out latent: test R2 (mean over dimensions) 0.488 on TACO, 0.345 on ARCTIC; pooled 0.500 vs 0.380; train-mean reference RMSE 0.993 vs 0.910.
Teacher-latent decoder floor: 0.505 (TACO) vs 0.694 (ARCTIC) for the new decoder; the floor moved +1.0 % ('similar') on TACO and +2.1 % ('better') on ARCTIC with the larger decoder.

Random-perturbation share of the predicted-latent error: 78-84 % on TACO, 84-90 % on ARCTIC; on ARCTIC the Gaussian-perturbed latent through the old decoder is only 'similar' to the predicted latent (interval includes 0), on TACO it is 'better'.
New vs old decoder on identical perturbed teacher latents (not part of the rule fixed in advance): 'better' in 4 of 4 comparisons on TACO, in 2 of 4 on ARCTIC.

Persistence baseline (C_t = s_0): 3.539 on TACO (far above every model); 2.242 on ARCTIC, only slightly above M1 / M2 (2.157 / 2.158) with overlapping intervals and no paired test; in ARCTIC frames 1-8 persistence (1.345) is below M2 (1.537) and M1 (1.600).
Held-out shrinkage probe: best factors all 1.0 on TACO; 0.9 / 0.9 / 1.0 / 1.0 / 1.0 on ARCTIC (test change +0.0008, similar).

ARCTIC test set: 21 of the 44 test takes are of a subject that is not in the training set; both ARCTIC failure examples shown in the report are of that subject. TACO has 186 test takes, ARCTIC 44, so ARCTIC intervals are wider.

Budget-parity check of the direct model (stopped unfinished, validation only): on ARCTIC the retrained M0 was already below the reused M0's best validation loss (0.9648 vs 0.9764), on TACO not (0.2303 vs 0.2223); the reused M0 may understate the direct model on ARCTIC only.
Frame-to-frame behaviour vs M1: on TACO M2's dense frame-to-frame change is closer to the data (deviation +23.5 % better); on ARCTIC it is further (-16.9 % worse, M2 moves more than the data).
do_not_claim: 'Decoder mismatch is not the bottleneck' / 'the decoder is excluded as the cause'. The source says 'Not shown ... No evidence was found that this mismatch caused the failure': only two extra blocks at width 256, a longer budget, selection on the dense loss and two small held-out probes were tested; a wider decoder and a decoder trained on many held-out predictions were not.
'A jointly trained decoder was compared with a frozen decoder.' M1 was already trained end to end on the predicted z; M2 differs in capacity, budget and selection, changed together.

'M2 equals M1' or 'no difference at all'. The verdict 'similar' is for the dense error under the 2 % + interval rule; on TACO the interval excludes 0, and participation and frames 1-8 are 'better' on both datasets while the ARCTIC frame-to-frame deviation is 'worse'.

'The TACO improvement is not significant' or, conversely, 'M2 improves on M1 on TACO'. It is resolved (interval excludes 0) and below the size threshold fixed in advance; one seed, 'a second seed could move it to either side'.
'The TACO gain comes from the larger decoder.' It is absent at a matched step and the report reads it as travelling with the predicted latent; selection, capacity and budget are not separated.
'The old and the new decoder produce the same maps.' They reach the same dense error on the same predicted latent.
'The decoder never saw test-sized latent errors during training.' It did in roughly its first thousand steps.
'M2 was trained much longer (100 k steps).' Both M2 runs stopped by the patience rule at 25 000 steps and were selected at step 7000 / 8000.

'The remaining bottleneck is proven to be z trajectory prediction.' The source says 'Most likely yes' and that the latent error cannot be separated from the decoder's sensitivity to it; a second, smaller part is the first frames, where the latent path cannot continue s_0.
'Random latent noise explains 78-90 % of the teacher-to-predicted gap.' Those shares are of the predicted-latent dense error, not of the gap.
'The temporal network memorises the training set and that causes the failure' as an established cause, or any claim about regularisation, data size or model size fixing it: no such ablation was run.

'Held-out adaptation of the decoder does not help' as a general statement. Two small probes on 141 / 106 validation sequences found no gain; Probe A chose zero steps (likely overfitting, fitting-fold error not recorded) and 'cannot bound what a decoder trained on many held-out predictions could do'.
'The teacher z error 0.51 / 0.69 is what a better z predictor would achieve at generation time.' The teacher z* is computed from the true future frames; it is a decoder floor.

'z-mediated generation is better for structure' without the qualifiers: TACO only, already true for M1 before the decoder changes, arising only from frame 17 on, with frames 1-8 worse than the direct model; on ARCTIC there is no structural advantage and the amount is worse.
'z-mediated models beat the persistence baseline on ARCTIC.' No paired test exists; 2.158 vs 2.242 with overlapping intervals, and persistence is lower in frames 1-8.
'ARCTIC is exactly 14 % worse than direct prediction' as a property of the method: the reused direct model may understate direct prediction on ARCTIC (budget-parity run stopped unfinished).
'The Stage-1 z is a poor representation' or 'z is at fault'. The source: 'The Stage-1 z is not shown to be at fault'.
'Decoder adaptation cannot beat the direct model' as a fact. It is an ideal-predictor argument in the report ('an argument, not a measurement').

'This result shows that a stateful / recurrent z model will fix the problem' or presenting the stateful-z experiment as a result: the report says 'Proposed, not shown'; it is a motivated current hypothesis.
Any pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC number, or any OakInk2 statement for these blocks.
'Wrench error measures human intent'; wrench relative L1 is a proxy for functional grasp capability.
Reading the overlapping unpaired intervals of the per-model bars as the test: the verdicts come from paired differences on identical sequences.
Results for the optional models M3 (decoder also fed the teacher latent) and M0r (direct model retrained): both were stopped unfinished and have validation-log numbers only, no test evaluation.

attached_by_the_verifier: The page's planned message 'decoder mismatch is not the main bottleneck' is stronger than the source. Report Appendix B Q1: 'Not shown ... No evidence was found that this mismatch caused the failure.' Tested: two extra blocks at width 256, a longer schedule, selection on the dense loss, two small held-out probes. Not tested: a wider decoder (512-768), the 4-block control under the M2 protocol, a decoder trained on many held-out predictions. The block heading has to carry this limit (the extractor has it only under do_not_claim).

The framing 'old decoder versus the jointly adapted decoder' is wrong for this study: M1 was already trained end to end on the predicted z. M2 differs by three changes made together (decoder 4 -> 6 blocks, 100 k schedule with no stop before 25 k, selection on validation L_C). Both M2 runs stopped by patience at 25 000 steps and were selected at step 7000 / 8000.

Prose versus table: report.md rounds the TACO M2-vs-M1 reduction to '2.0%' in section 11 ('That is the 2.0% of Section 9') and in the section 14 table ('+2.0%, similar (close call)'). The table value is rel_improvement 0.019623757636585915 (1.96 %), below the 0.02 threshold. Use 1.96 %; '2.0 %' would read as meeting the threshold.

Sign convention must be stated on the page: raw differences are first model minus second (negative = first lower); percentages are 'relative improvement' (positive = first model lower error). '+1.96 %' is a reduction, '-14.19 %' is worse.

No horizon figure was delivered. The TACO 'similar' dense mean against M0 hides a split (paired_comparisons.csv E_C_h*: frames 1-8 -36.5 % worse, 9-16 -6.7 % worse, 17-32 similar, 33-48 +4.0 % better, 49-63 +4.5 % better); ARCTIC is worse in every bin (-45.6 % to -8.1 %). If the page states 'TACO similar with better structure', this caveat has to be in the text, or a figure built from horizon_metrics.csv.

Caveat for F3-subB not delivered: the decoder fed the TEACHER z* is also about three times worse on test than on the 160 training sequences (new decoder 0.179 -> 0.505 TACO, 0.234 -> 0.694 ARCTIC; decoder_diagnostic.csv; training subset has no interval). The figure f3subb_dense_train_vs_test shows it. The page should not attribute the whole train-test difference of the decoded error to the predicted latent.

Context for the train-test latent gap that the report gives and the entries omit: the temporal network has about 68 M parameters (67,923,712 backbone) and the training sets have 1,312 (TACO) and 1,005 (ARCTIC) sequences (report section 11); the dense loss term uses 4 random future frames per sequence per step while L_z uses all 63 (report section 17).

Probe caveat wording: 'the validation contact maps, which no compared model has seen' comes from the zj_probe.py docstring. Every compared model used the validation set for checkpoint selection, so write 'trained on', not 'seen'. Also use the report's sentence ('cannot bound ...'), not the docstring's older 'bound the benefit from above'.

The extractor's list of resolved M2-vs-M1 secondary differences is not exhaustive. Also in paired_comparisons.csv: TACO frames 9-16 better (+2.25 %), TACO deviation of the dense frame-to-frame change better (+23.5 %) and of the R2 change better (+6.8 %).

No figure for the held-out probes (heldout_probe.csv is text-only evidence), and none of the report's own plots (fig4_z_prediction.png, fig5_decoder_mismatch.png, fig8_train_vs_heldout.png) was recommended; the module redraws their content, so this is not a gap unless the page wants the originals.
